title: Many voices
hookLine: no single leader speaks for all Sikhs; the Granth and the sangat hold the panth together

lines: CAN I SPEAK TO THE HEAD?
A GRANTHI, A COMMITTEE, A TAKHT.
cards: A reporter calls a gurdwara with a simple request. Can she speak to the head of the Sikh religion? The volunteer who picks up the phone pauses.
There's a granthi who reads from the Granth here. There's a committee that runs the building. There's the Akal Takht in Amritsar, whose word carries real weight.

But a single person who speaks for every Sikh on earth? The volunteer tries to explain, and the reporter keeps waiting for a name. Today is why there isn't one, and what holds the panth together instead.

teach.b: Sikh tradition says that before Guru Gobind Singh died, he ended the line of human Gurus.
From then on, the Guru would be the Granth, the scripture, and the Khalsa Panth, the community of Sikhs gathered in the Guru's presence. Sikhs speak of Guru Granth and Guru Panth.
That choice shapes everything this week has been about.
There are respected bodies. The Akal Takht issues edicts, and they carry weight across the panth. The Shiromani Committee manages historic gurdwaras and published the code of conduct.
Taksals and jathas have their own teachers. Local sangats run their own gurdwaras. But none of these is a single head over every Sikh.

Authority is spread out, and it's meant to sit under the Granth, not over it. So how does a panth with many voices stay one? On Ang 72, Guru Nanak asks, here in paraphrase, how is the true congregation known?

teach.h: WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.
teach.b: And answers: it is where the one Name is spoken. Not where one leader stands. Where the Name is.
So a small sangat in a rented hall abroad, a great crowd at the Harmandir, and a family reading together at home can each be the sangat. Many voices is not a design flaw.
It's what happens when the Guru is a book everyone can open, and the community is everyone who opens it.
The voices sometimes clash. They also keep each other honest.

how: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru and the Khalsa Panth as the community gathered around it; bodies like the Akal Takht and the Shiromani Committee carry weight, and local sangats run their own gurdwaras, but no single leader speaks for all Sikhs.

o: no single leader speaks for every Sikh
a council that votes on every Sikh rule
a choir singing in several languages

games.q: inside many voices: tap the pairs.
p: the true congregation: where the Name is

s: Sikhs have one head who speaks for all
authority is spread out, and meant to sit under the Granth.
Gurbani tests a true gathering by whether the one Name is spoken there
a small sangat in a rented hall can be a true sangat
the test is the Name, not the size or the building.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, and someone asks how to know a true congregation. what do you say?
o: where the one Name is spoken.
games.why: on Ang 72, the true sangat is known by the Name spoken there. that's part of why many voices can still be one panth.

practice: Think of whose voice is usually missing from the circles you're in, someone younger or older, someone quieter, someone from a different neighborhood or kind of work, and bring one such person to mind.
Hold them there a while with real attention, and if you pray, hold them before Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Many voices. No single leader speaks for every Sikh; the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat, gathered around the Name, hold the panth together. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the congregation, the gathered community.

carryVoice: Your line: many voices, one guru. Where the Name is spoken, there's the sangat. Same time tomorrow.
